transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-03-05 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Gupta (Redwood SE), Priya Raman (Argon CTO), Liam O'Connor (Lead ML Eng), Zoe Park (Security Ops)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Discussed migration from OpenAI/Anthropic to Redwood Dedicated; major themes were eval parity, runtime compatibility with vLLM and TGI, and security controls for PII. Agreed to run a POC and exchange sizing/benchmark artifacts.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro from our side — i'm maya, account exec, and samir is our solutions engineer. how about a quick round from argon?
[00:12] Priya Raman: hi i'm priya, cto at argon. we run a mix of openai and anthropic models in prod for our customer support summarization and routing.
[00:20] Liam O'Connor: liam here, lead ml eng. i own infra for model calls and the inference pipeline.
[00:25] Zoe Park: and i'm zoe, security ops, i'll be looking at compliance and KMS stuff.
[00:30] Samir Gupta: great, thanks. the goal here is to understand your current stack, the pain points, and whether dedicated or private makes sense. quick question: are you currently using function calling and streaming in prod?
[00:44] Liam O'Connor: yes to both. streaming for low-latency UX and function-call style interface for structured outputs. we also use OpenAI for most user-facing flows and Anthropic for some internal safety models.
[01:05] Maya Chen: perfect. can you share rough qps and token profiles? even ballparks help with sizing.
[01:10] Liam O'Connor: total qps is around 30 rps, peaks to about 80 during business hours; average request is 600 tokens in and 250 out. monthly tokens around 450M.
[01:30] Priya Raman: main drivers for looking at migration are cost — the per-token variability is killing predictability — and we need better control over PII retention. also curious about latency improvements.
[01:45] Samir Gupta: makes sense. a lot of customers come to dedicated for cost predictability and control. for latency — depending on model and quantization — we often get 2x improvements vs public endpoints because of optimized kernels, batching control and KV cache strategies.
[02:05] Zoe Park: security wise, we need SOC2 compliance, SSO integration, and our keys must be in our KMS. we also have data residency constraints for EU customers.
[02:20] Maya Chen: we support SSO/SAML, customer-managed KMS, and private deployments with VPC peering. we can scope SOC2 paperwork into the enterprise pack.
[02:35] Liam O'Connor: big question — compatibility. we prototype locally with vLLM and sometimes TGI. will our prompt engineering and evals port over? tokenizer differences, sampling seeds, and even small tokenization changes have bitten us before.
[02:53] Samir Gupta: good point. we care a lot about eval parity. quick summary: model weights are the same for a given open model, but tokenization and runtime (vllm/tgi) differences can change outputs. our approach is twofold: 1) we provide a tokenizer parity checklist and scripts to compare tokenization and decoding, 2) we run an eval harness during POC to compare outputs across a representative prompt set.
[03:20] Priya Raman: do you run vLLM under the hood in Redwood Dedicated? we currently have some internal tooling around vLLM for memory efficiency.
[03:30] Samir Gupta: we don't rely on exactly one runtime. our serving runtime has multiple execution backends and kernel selections; we also support serving artifacts compatible with vLLM/TGI workflows. the important part is that we expose identical inference APIs and can run the eval harness across backends to flag regressions.
[03:56] Liam O'Connor: another small but painful thing — function calling schema and structured outputs. we've seen differences in how model returns slots and tools are invoked between providers.
[04:10] Maya Chen: we support function/tool calling and structured output. during POC we'll include your function calling test cases.
[04:20] Zoe Park: what about streaming consistency? we rely on chunked tokens to update the UI.
[04:29] Samir Gupta: streaming is supported; we have both chunked and event-stream styles. we'll validate end-to-end during the POC so you don't hit surprises.
[04:40] Priya Raman: latency targets — we want p95 under 300ms for small completions (<=128 tokens) and sub-second for mid-length. is that realistic on Dedicated?
[04:55] Samir Gupta: for smaller models and optimized quantization, yes. for large 70B-class models it's harder. we can size GPU pools accordingly — small model variants or quantized runs often hit your p95. we'll run benchmarks with your prompt set to validate.
[05:15] Liam O'Connor: about quantization — we use q4/q5 variants in prod. how does Redwood manage quantized model variants and fallbacks?
[05:25] Maya Chen: we maintain model catalog with verified quantization profiles. routing policies can fallback to a compatible variant if capacity is constrained. you can pin version and fallback rules in rollout configs.
[05:40] Priya Raman: cost — how do you price Dedicated? flat monthly for reserved capacity plus overage?
[05:48] Maya Chen: typically reserved capacity with monthly/annual commits; we'll send a sizing + pricing spreadsheet. there are also add-ons for observability retention and premium SLAs.
[06:00] Zoe Park: audit logs — do you retain token-level traces for debugging? we have privacy concerns around storing raw user content.
[06:10] Samir Gupta: we can do token-level traces in your private control plane, but redaction and retention policies are configurable. for PII we recommend on-the-fly redaction and storing only hashes, or forwarding logs to your SIEM.
[06:30] Priya Raman: can we run a side-by-side eval: our current OpenAI+Anthropic baseline vs Redwood Dedicated? we need objective metrics for quality parity and cost.
[06:40] Samir Gupta: yes — we'll run an eval run with your prompt set, compute similarity metrics (ROUGE/BERTScore/embedding-based), and also measure latency/cost per token. we'll share the harness and reproducible run notes.
[06:55] Liam O'Connor: one wrinkle: we sometimes host in Azure and use Azure OpenAI for some flows. will Redwood Dedicated integrate with our Azure VNet or do we need to route through public egress?
[07:08] Maya Chen: for Private deployments we can do VPC peering and private connectivity. Dedicated in a cloud region can be set up with private networking. we'll map your network ops requirements in the POC kickoff.
[07:25] Zoe Park: regulatory note — for EU customers we need data residency in eu-west-1. can you guarantee that for Dedicated?
[07:33] Samir Gupta: yes, region pinning is supported. for Private on-prem we can also do a full air-gapped deployment if needed.
[07:45] Priya Raman: integration — our stack is in python, using the openai client and some in-house wrappers. migration risk is the SDK and small API shape differences.
[07:58] Maya Chen: our SDKs map closely to OpenAI shapes (completion/chat/embeddings) and we provide migration guides and samples. for function calling we try to be compatible, but we'll validate with your tests.
[08:15] Liam O'Connor: how about rate limiting and throttling? our flow has bursts and we want graceful degradation rather than 429s in the UI.
[08:27] Samir Gupta: we support configurable rate-limits and graceful degradation policies — burst queues, queuing strategies, and automatic fallback to lower-cost model variants.
[08:40] Priya Raman: more on compatibility — we've built evals that rely on deterministic seeds for sampling. getting bit by non-deterministic sampling across providers has caused flaky tests.
[08:52] Samir Gupta: we'll document determinism guarantees per model/config. some sampling engines can be seeded, others approximate. as part of POC we'll lock sampling params and run multiple seeds to measure variance.
[09:10] Maya Chen: ops question — what does on-call look like for Dedicated customers?
[09:17] Samir Gupta: Dedicated customers have 24/7 on-call with tiered SLAs depending on contract. ops escalations go through a dedicated CSM and infra pager on our side.
[09:30] Zoe Park: security posture — can you confirm encryption at rest, in transit, and customer-managed keys?
[09:38] Maya Chen: yes to all three. we also provide audit logs, RBAC, and optional HSM integrations for high-sensitivity keys.
[09:50] Priya Raman: ok, realistic POC timeline?
[09:55] Maya Chen: typical is 2–3 weeks for an initial eval: week 0 onboarding + network setup, week 1 run evals and latency/cost benchmarks, week 2 iterate on models and routing. for deeper security reviews we extend.
[10:15] Liam O'Connor: do you have an example eval report? we want to see how parities are reported and what pass/fail criteria look like.
[10:24] Samir Gupta: yes, we'll share a sample eval report and the threshold configs we use for quality regression alerts.
[10:35] Priya Raman: question about shared artifacts — if you send the pricing spreadsheet and the eval harness, are there any NDAs we need to sign first?
[10:44] Maya Chen: we can share non-sensitive docs right away; for sample code or internal benchmarks we typically do an NDA. we can start with the public materials and tighten up as needed.
[10:58] Liam O'Connor: any customers who've migrated from OpenAI + in-house vLLM to your Dedicated offering? curious about their experience with parity.
[11:10] Samir Gupta: yes — a couple of customers ran side-by-side POCs. common themes: initial tokenization diffs and sampling variance, but after quantization/profile tuning and small prompt tweaks they hit parity and saw cost improvements. we'll share anonymized case notes.
[11:35] Priya Raman: about the POC compute — do you recommend we bring our own model weights or use your curated catalog?
[11:45] Samir Gupta: both options available. many customers use our curated catalog for speed; if you have licensed weights we'll work through deployment notes to ensure compatibility.
[11:58] Zoe Park: from a compliance angle, if we bring our own weights, does Redwood still access the data? we need guarantees about control plane metadata.
[12:10] Maya Chen: in Private/on-prem deployments the control plane can be customer-managed. even in Dedicated we can limit control plane visibility and put logs in your SIEM. we'll map that out in the security review.
[12:28] Liam O'Connor: ok, want to call out a specific technical concern: our current TGI-based stack uses a custom kv-cache for long conversations. will that translate?
[12:40] Samir Gupta: we have KV cache management and APIs for prefix cache; we may need to map your semantics but we've migrated other customers with custom KV store patterns. part of the SE scope will be to validate cache semantics.
[12:58] Maya Chen: sounds like we have a reasonable plan. recap the open items to confirm?
[13:05] Priya Raman: i'll send anonymized prompt set and traffic shape.
[13:10] Liam O'Connor: i'll add the tokenizer edge cases and the function calling tests.
[13:15] Zoe Park: i'll list SOC2 scope and confirm KMS details.
[13:20] Samir Gupta: we'll send the eval harness, tokenizer parity checklist, and a proposed POC runbook.
[13:28] Maya Chen: and i'll send pricing + Dedicated sizing.
[13:35] Priya Raman: any blockers on our end for starting the POC next week?
[13:40] Maya Chen: network peering approvals and an NDA if you want the full bench artifacts — both doable in parallel.
[13:50] Priya Raman: we'll try for 2026-03-10 for kickoff.
[13:55] Liam O'Connor: one last quick question — telemetry and monitoring: we need token-level latency percentiles in your console, ideally broken down by model and route.
[14:08] Samir Gupta: our console provides per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and tracing hooks. we can onboard a test route to demonstrate.
[14:20] Zoe Park: who is the redwood engineer to work with for network/security?
[14:25] Maya Chen: samir will be primary SE. i'll introduce a solutions architect if needed.
[14:35] Priya Raman: thanks all.
[14:38] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the artifacts and proposed calendar invites.
